strengths: Well-motivated benchmark addressing a real gap in agent code security evaluation for repository-level, multi-file tasks with realistic complexity (150K LoC context, 172 edited lines, 77 CWEs across 10 domains)
Thoughtful automated curation pipeline with adaptive masking, description generation, and verification ensuring task integrity and scalability to new vulnerabilities
Significant and striking findings: 80%+ of functionally correct agent solutions are insecure, revealing a critical gap that has practical importance for vibe coding adoption
Comprehensive evaluation across 9 agent/LLM combinations with rigorous metrics (SECPASS ⊥ FUNCPASS) that disentangle security from functional capability
Clear, well-structured presentation with effective figures and concrete qualitative case studies (D.1-D.3) illustrating real security vulnerabilities
Honest discussion of limitations (Python-only, test-based evaluation) and preliminary nature of mitigation strategies
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: curation pipeline applies existing LLM techniques (masking, generation, verification) in a straightforward manner; core insight of using vulnerability fixes as task sources is sensible but not surprising

Security evaluation relies entirely on test-based proxies: average 3.7 tests per task is modest, and test-based evaluation may miss subtle exploits, edge cases, and sophisticated attacks not explicitly tested

Critical absence of human baseline: abstract mentions humans generated vulnerable code on these tasks but provides no quantitative comparison, making it unclear if agent performance is worse than human programmers

Shallow exploration of mitigation strategies (Section 5): only three simple prompting approaches tested with no investigation of root causes, no analysis of why security guidance reduces functionality, and no exploration of alternative approaches (tools, fine-tuning, multi-agent)

Python-only scope limits generalizability across programming languages and security domains with different characteristics (e.g., C/Rust memory safety vulnerabilities differ from Python security concerns)

Curation process dependencies: three curation steps use SWE-Agent itself, creating circular dependency; no ablation study or sensitivity analysis on masking/description quality effects on downstream evaluation

Missing statistical analysis: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests despite evaluating stochastic LLMs; unclear if observed differences between agents are statistically meaningful

Unexplained findings: Gemini 3 Pro shows 195% functional improvement but only 57% security improvement (Table 5), suggesting possible artifacts or "secure by accident" patterns that deserve deeper analysis

strengths: Addresses critical and timely problem of evaluating security in AI-based code generation, highly relevant given widespread vibe coding adoption
Novel benchmark with sophisticated automatic curation pipeline: iterative masking, task generation, and verification using repository-level code with real vulnerability fixes
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 3 agent frameworks and 3 frontier LLMs, with stratified analysis by CWE type revealing complementary strengths and blind spots
Significant empirical finding: 80%+ of functionally correct solutions from best agent are insecure, with concrete real-world implications for practitioners
Excellent presentation with detailed case studies illustrating concrete security risks (timing attacks, CRLF injection, XSS, session replay) grounded in actual vulnerabilities
Substantial scale and realism: 200 tasks covering 77 CWEs across 10 domains, averaging 172 lines of edits across multiple files in ~150K LOC repositories
Repository-level tasks (not just functions/files) better reflect real-world vibe coding compared to existing single-file/function benchmarks
weaknesses: Language and domain scope limited to Python (only 3,000 of 20,000 commits mined) and repository-level tasks; unclear how results generalize to other languages and programming scenarios common in vibe coding practice

Test-based security evaluation relies on human-written unit tests which may miss many exploit modalities; no dynamic testing, fuzzing, or adversarial evaluation; acknowledged in appendix that benchmark 'does not claim coverage of all exploit modalities'
Filtering process from ~3,000 Python commits to 200 final tasks not clearly explained; filtering criteria, stratification strategy, and potential biases in task selection are unclear

Potential circularity in benchmark construction: using LLMs (Claude 4 Sonnet) for masking, generating task descriptions, and verifying consistency could introduce systematic biases and reduce task difficulty

Weak exploration of mitigation strategies: only three simple prompting approaches tested; no investigation of training-based solutions (fine-tuning, RL), runtime monitoring, formal verification, or tool use (symbolic execution, static analysis)

Evaluation methodology limitations: pass@1 metric doesn't reflect iterative refinement that users might perform; generic security reminder added to baseline weakens interpretation; no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals; single run per task; sample size of 200 modest for stratification across 77 CWEs

Incomplete analysis of security-functionality tradeoff: why does security prompting cause functional regression? Limited systematic categorization of failure modes; no comparison with human expert performance; limited discussion of what makes the 10.5% secure solutions different

Reproducibility concerns: precise model versions not fully specified; complex Docker environment building described across appendices; cost analysis (token usage) not discussed; heavy reliance on appendices

strengths: Addresses timely, important problem: vibe coding adoption is widespread (75% of developers) but security implications poorly understood; paper documents concerning gap between functional correctness (57%) and security (11.8%)

Rigorous benchmark construction with real vulnerabilities: multi-stage curation pipeline from actual vulnerability fixes prevents artificial/synthetic weaknesses; verification steps prevent information leakage; execution-based validation with Docker

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 12 agentic settings (3 frameworks × 4 LLMs), 186 tasks across 79 CWE types and 10 domains, clear metrics (FuncPass, SecPass, SecPass⊥FuncPass) that properly isolate security from functionality

Concrete case studies with real exploits: Appendix D provides detailed vulnerability examples (timing side-channels, CRLF injection, XSS, session fixation) showing how functionally plausible code can be exploitable
Well-designed verification methodology: iterative feature masking with line-by-line linking to requirements (Figure 7) elegantly ensures security fixes not leaked into task descriptions
Strong presentation and reproducibility commitments: clear writing, informative figures, extensive appendices with prompts and statistics, promised open release of code and dataset
weaknesses: Limited language scope (Python ≥3.7 only) severely restricts generalizability; unclear how findings transfer to other languages with different vulnerability patterns and security cultures

Test-based security proxy has inherent limitations: unit tests may miss exploitable vulnerabilities; 44% of security tests may miss edge-case implementations; inter-rater agreement for test verification not reported

Benchmark construction concerns: automated mask generation via LLM could subtly leak security hints; 2.2% of tasks with CWE-noinfo/CWE-Other; small sample sizes in some CWE categories limit statistical power for stratified analysis

Weak mitigation strategies analysis: only preliminary approaches tested (self-selection, oracle) that both degrade functionality while providing minimal security gains; no exploration of sophisticated solutions (security-aware training, tool use, structured prompting); root causes of functionality-security trade-off not well explained

Insufficient root cause analysis: limited investigation into *why* agents fail at security; no deep categorization of failure modes by CWE type; Section 4.3 qualitative analysis limited to one example; Table 6 shows CWE identification recall only 0.667 but minimal follow-up

Human verification details sparse: inter-rater agreement not reported; number of annotators unclear; disagreement resolution process underspecified; Appendix B.5 mentions revisions without quantitative metrics

Modest benchmark size (186 tasks) with thin stratification: when divided across 79 CWE types and 10 domains, some cells in Table 4 show 0%, single-digit percentages, limiting ability to draw statistical conclusions for categories

Missing context for evaluation: no human performance baseline (even informal); limited error analysis beyond case studies; no exploration of whether agents could be trained on SUSVIBES to improve security

strengths: Addresses timely and critical problem: vibe coding adoption is increasing while security remains understudied
Rigorous benchmark construction with multiple validation layers: execution-based validation, expert human review, and deliberate decoupling from ground-truth implementations
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 12 agentic settings with 186 real-world tasks covering 79 CWE types (7× more than existing benchmarks)
Striking and actionable findings: 79.3% of functionally correct solutions contain vulnerabilities, clearly demonstrating the security-functionality gap
High-quality tasks reflecting real-world complexity: 175 lines average, 1.8 files, 33% requiring multi-file reasoning
Well-designed curation pipeline with adaptive verification ensures descriptions match secure implementations without leaking security requirements
Thorough experimental analysis including CWE-specific performance breakdown, domain-specific evaluation, and qualitative case studies with concrete attack scenarios
Excellent documentation and reproducibility: detailed appendices with prompts, pipeline statistics, and methodology
weaknesses: Limited scope: Python ≥3.7 repositories only; generalizability to other languages and paradigms unclear
Test-based security evaluation has inherent limitations: 44% of security tests only partially cover alternative secure implementations; may miss vulnerabilities not captured by tests
No human developer baseline: stronger comparative analysis would strengthen claims about agent performance gap
Underdeveloped mitigation strategies: preliminary prompting approaches tested show that simple solutions don't work, but limited exploration of why or better alternatives
Heavy reliance on LLMs for task curation: mask generation and description writing use SWE-AGENT instances, introducing potential biases
Limited systematic analysis of failure modes: why do agents consistently miss certain security patterns? Multi-file complexity drops are noted but not deeply investigated
Incomplete discussion of complementary model strengths: Figure 4 shows models excel at different CWE categories but lacks explanation or suggestions for ensemble approaches
Missing comparisons: no evaluation against static analysis tools, fuzzing, or other security validation approaches; no discussion of hybrid agent-tool systems
Critical dataset links appear broken/redacted in submission: 'available at The leaderboard is a' sentence incomplete
Minor statistical gaps: inter-annotator agreement metrics for human verification not reported; LLM hyperparameter specifications (temperature, etc.) not fully documented
